source.title: Open Problems in Relational Quantum Mechanics

accepted.question_text: If relational quantum mechanics rejects observer-independent quantum states and instead treats the state of a system as relative to an observing or interacting physical system, what explanatory work does this relativization of states actually perform, and in what precise sense does it improve our understanding of quantum phenomena rather than merely redescribing them?

evidence.quote: Here I argue – mainly through an analysis of the so-called third person problem – that it is far from clear what a relativization of states to observers exactly achieves and in what sense such an approach really advances our understanding of the peculiar features of quantum phenomena: therefore, in this respect, RQM still faces open problems.

In the present paper I will argue that both claims (i) and (ii) are controversial, and that this brings to bear on the locality issue within RQM: as such, RQM still faces open problems, since it is far from clear what a relativization of states to observers exactly achieves and in what sense such an approach really advances our understanding of the peculiar features of quantum phenomena.

accepted.question_text: Can the "third person problem" genuinely justify the fundamental claim of relational quantum mechanics that quantum states must be relativized to observers, once the measurement process is described without ambiguity and the comparison between the sequence in which observer O records a definite outcome and the sequence in which observer P models the combined system is made fully explicit?

evidence.quote: To sum up: the "third person problem" is allegedly one of the cornerstones of RQM, and the main argument underlying it is meant to support the shift to a fundamental relativization of states of quantum physical systems to observers. The formulation itself of the problem, however, seems to be based on a basic ambiguity, affecting the very description of a measurement process provided by different observers. If one tries to remove the ambiguity by sharpening the description, the alleged difference between E and E′ appears to evaporate and the motivation for the relativization gets considerably weaker.

accepted.question_text: Can relational quantum mechanics give a justified account of state reduction in measurement, including when all systems are treated quantum mechanically, or does it merely attach observer-relative indices to states while leaving the collapse process unexplained and the measurement problem unresolved?

evidence.quote: Even if the description is supposed to be relativized to an E-observer, RQM inherits from standard QM the state reduction process: as a consequence, RQM shares with standard QM the controversial status of state reduction.

Moreover, even if we set aside the ambiguity inherent in the formulation of the third person problem, it is hard to see how even a fundamental relativization of states of quantum physical systems to observers in RQM might make sense without further justification of the collapse process, that remains unexplained in the interpretation: hence, the measurement problem stricto sensu remains unsolved in the interpretation.

accepted.question_text: In Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen and Bell-type cases, can relational quantum mechanics preserve locality merely by denying observer-independent properties, or must it still accept a non-local dependence because standard quantum-mechanical probabilities violate outcome independence even if parameter independence is preserved?

evidence.quote: If this is true, then we must acknowledge that what the Bell theorem is about is nonlocality. In this sense, the simple decision to drop observer-independence of states and values of physical quantities can not be in itself a first step toward the preservation of locality within the quantum domain, because in this case the lack of observer-independence turns out to be a ‘challenge’ to a condition which is not an assumption of Bell’s theorem.

But if this is true, RQM appears then to be forced to accept some form of non-locality in quantum phenomena, namely the non-local sort of dependence that shows up in the above mentioned violation of outcome-dependence, which is a probabilistic condition.
